title: Television needs to stop following the blockbuster model of movies and return to annual release of seasons

commenti.body:
Game of thrones used to be able to have a release a year. But somehow that became too hard at the end? It's strange. 

This year will be off no matter what though due to the writers strike.

The Sopranos had a year+ gap between seasons 4 & 5 and a damn near 2-year gap between 5 & 6. The Wire was similar. Shows take gaps for a myriad of reasons - strikes, contract disputes, scheduling conflicts, etc.

Mad Men had a big gap as well. But, to OPs point, those were the exceptions and not the rule. Those gaps were really big deals back then with lots of stories and such written about it and discussed. Now, it's no big deal when a show has a 2-year break.

I mean, if the pace of work to maintain that release schedule isn't tenable, something has to give eventually; something like leaving coffee cups in the shot and nobody on the entire cast and crew notices happen because everyone is beyond exhausted.

I'd rather have shorter seasons released less often by crews given enough time and money to have quality of life

Yep. In the UK we've had 3 Prime Ministers since the first season of House of Dragons. 

This phenomenon is impacting most pop cultural output now - music and games notably too. People just need to calm the hell down with perfection, concern around audience expectation and well... profit, profit, profit. Self consciousness kills art.

>But I think maybe Television needs to step back from the blockbuster model and get back to the character driven, writer focused medium that it has been.

Firstly, you keep calling it "the blockbuster model", when it isn't confined to blockbuster-like big productions only, and isn't caused solely by inflated post-production schedules.

Secondly, you never really presented an argument that television used to be a "character driven, writer focused medium", and has since stopped being one, let alone that it stopped being such a medium specifically because of what you call "the blockbuster model".

The only argument you did present against "the blockbuster model" is:

>having this long period of time between seasons of a show means that you forget all the plot points, you lose your investment in the characters and you just give up on keeping up with the show

Which is not universally true (if people did just give up on shows because of long hiatuses, then production studios would have stopped doing them because they'd be losing money) and doesn't reflect real life viewing habits of most people.

I'd say that the whole discussion on hiatuses is a bit reductive, and a remnant of the concept of "TV as a medium for water cooler moments that should just aim to maximize people watching an episode premiere" instead of what television serials should be regarded as - a narrative art form, just like cinema. And if it takes more time to make a season, then so be it. Creatives shouldn't be overworked or shackled to a single production's yearly shooting schedule for 5-8 years just so that fans don't havs to wait an extra 6 to 12 months between seasons.

And don't forget that the people watching a show as it releases will be the absolute minority of people who end up watching that show - a majority of viewers for any show will never know what a hiatus for that show looked like, because they'll watch it once it has all finished airing.
Maybe they want you to rewarch every 2 years because it earns them more money. It's slighy wild theory but not that far off.

>And if it takes more time to make a season, then so be it. Creatives shouldn't be overworked or shackled to a single production's yearly shooting schedule for 5-8 years just so that fans don't havs to wait an extra 6 to 12 months between seasons.

Exactly this! I have no idea why there have been so many complaints about television shows taking 2 year breaks. As someone who watches anime and knowing how overworked the anime industry is, I'm happy to wait between seasons for good work and for creatives to have enough time to do their work. Kyoto Animation, which is my favourite animation studio regularly puts technically brilliant, visually gorgeous and also well-written and narratively compelling films and anime series and they unfortunately lost a huge chunk of their staff who perished during an arson attack in 2019. As fans of the studio's output, we understood that they had to delay their releases. We understood that they would take a long time to put out their next work. I waited 7-10 years for 2 of my favourite animes to get their new seasons released this year. 

There are always new people becoming fans and there are always fans that will stay on for a long time. If the series is good, people will stick around. 

For TV series these days, there are things like cast scheduling issues since so many people can't make money just doing a tv show so they're off doing other projects as soon as they can. Besides big scale shows like House of the Dragon that clearly need a long pre-production time due to the scale of their production, even tv shows like Interview with the Vampire with a smaller cast and lesser sets also take time to create the deeply beautiful sets they use and find the locations in Europe to shoot. I'm not sure what people want? The industry used to believe these type of these epic stories, or genre stories (especially those adapted from book series) could only be told in cinema, which meant a lot of cutting down of story. Television given more time and money to make stories that challenge the medium and its possibilities should be a good thing.

A fairer comparison would be a season per sequel. Most of the problems you outline exist between movie sequels as well, if they even manage to get one out.

The better option is to simply have a story with a beginning, middle, and end with any type of sequel being a gamble to the overall narrative. Most long running series do suffer an eventual dip in quality, including some of the greats like The Godfather or The Exorcist.
